title: "Honestly, I Am Terrified I Will End Up In Your Newsletter"
subtitle: An open letter to everybody who has the good sense to worry about satire... and assure you, it's not you I'm gonna make fun of.
text:
I need to explain something. This newsletter includes satirical content. Some individuals, and one very brave individual—who I won’t mention because that's the point—worry that I might skewer them! You know, with sass.

This perception? It is an unmitigated success for my overarching goal of encouraging compliance with all appropriate rules and regulations. However, it misses a little bit of the point.

I am child and adolescent psychiatrist. People ask me questions, at any given social event, about if they're going to screw up their kids.

And my answer to both worried parents and worried innovators is the same: if you're worrying, you're not the kind of person at risk.

People who “screw up their kids,” almost axiomatically, are not the people who are worried they will screw up their kids.

Similarly, the satire I write about Healthcare and innovation isn't funny if I make fun of somebody who's going to get the joke. It is a little bit like McSweeney's “open letters to individuals or entities highly unlikely to respond.”

When it comes to the objects of my ire, they share a crucial uniting feature: they don't get it.

If you're poking fun at someone who gets it, they are in on the joke. And I love sharing humor. I like laughing together. UnitedHealth Group, my regular proxy for all massive corporations that control Healthcare, is not an organization that has a sense of humor. There is nothing funny about United healthcare.

This impairment in a sense of irony leaves them open to

• making terrible decisions that have horrific impacts on the lives of patients and doctors,

• Leaves UHC breathtakingly open to satirical commentary.

Their podcast, I will point out, is unironically called “until it's fixed:”

You know, the unimaginable dream of taking some amount of money plus innovative ideas, let's say, oh, I don't know, $330 billion every single year in revenue and $4.something billion in profit last quarter? I wonder if there was some way we could take phenomenal amounts of money plus innovative ideas in healthcare and change anything? Probably not. It's just a crazy dream. But let's make a podcast about how hard that would be using our unbelievable technology and financial resources instead of changing anything?

Subscribe now

This is the kind of satire I'm talking about. UnitedHealthGroup is not a person. It's not reading my newsletter. There are good and decent people who work there. Maybe they are readers? I'm going to make fun of UnitedHealth group, because they have $330 billion in revenue. There is no solution to the problem of being the largest healthcare company on earth, there's only the relentless pursuit of getting even bigger. That’s not a problem for them.

There is nothing funny about an inter-planetary scale of revenue. This is why I have to laugh. We all have to laugh. And that can change our minds. Because when we don't take it very seriously, it is basically the red pill from the matrix. And maybe, just maybe, we can start thinking differently about what we should do.

If Neo had zero ability to take himself seriously, that might be me?

I mean, at this point

I don't even see the code any more, I just see the endless profits that prior authorization makes possible. I know what you are thinking. Because I am thinking it too.

Why didn’t I just take the blue pill and build a company for the purpose of getting acquired by Optum?

But I'm not here to drag you out of the matrix, I'm here to offer you a choice. With great power, there's some degree of responsibility, and I will abide by all appropriate rules and regulations when it comes to deploying that power. This is not in keeping with the Hippocratic Oath of satirists: first, make no fun of the sincere and good.

—Owen Scott Muir, M.D.
